papers.full_text: Conclusions and policy directionsThe health and care workforce policy-crisis calls for radical transformations in health policy and systems, moving the debate towards capacities and workforce-driven innovation. Four major strategic policy shifts are indicative to fully enhance and integrate the transformative workforce capacities.Establishing a multi-level participatory governance architecture that connects bottom-up capacities and self-efficacy of frontline workers with top-down strategic guidance, using existing knowledge and actionable policy solutions more coherently and effectively.Shifting health systems and the organization of care towards community- and primary care-centred approaches that are better able to stimulate bottom-up innovation and integrate workforce-driven knowledge strategically into wider health policy.Shifting workforce policy from technical approaches on human resources as part of infrastructures towards health and care workers as persons and the workforce as an essential pillar of health systems security and resilience.Improving data and research on workforce-driven innovation to create governance architectures capable of integrating transformative capacities, while ensuring regulation and strategic oversight of workforce stability and health system resilience. IntroductionChanging population health and new security threats require a resilient health and care workforce, yet health workers are exhausted, labour market capacities are decreasing, and a coherent workforce strategy is still lacking in most European countries. In this situation, workforce-driven stability and resilience may emerge bottom-up. However, these capacities are not well understood by health policy. Instead, health and care workers are mostly perceived as critical infrastructure and as a cost factor for health systems, obscuring the view of both the needs of individual health workers and their active role in health systems.This Viewpoint argues that the transformational capacities of the health and care workforce not only need greater attention but also require a new mindset of workforce policy. Bottom-up workforce-driven transformations are crucial for innovating health systems, supporting the implementation of policy reform and advancing equity and inclusiveness in the workforce itself and in healthcare provision. They can strengthen workforce stability, health system resilience and trust in governments and create co-benefits for other sectors. To unlock these capacities, workforce policies must shift from short-term technical crisis solutions towards a coherent strategy that looks beyond headcounts and acknowledges, in a comprehensive and intersectional way, the person behind every health worker, recognizing in most cases a woman and often a migrant.By focusing on the workforce as an active player and an important pillar of health systems, this Viewpoint highlights new capacities for workforce stability and health systems resilience, calling for policy shifts from crisis towards capacities and implementation [1–3]. The Viewpoint introduces changes driven by knowledge and experience of frontline workers, highlights transformational effects in health systems, and explores supportive governance structures for these capacities to flourish. Health and care workforce as an active stakeholder and innovator of health systemsWorkforce-driven capacities are highly flexible, and the transformative effects in health systems are diverse and context-dependent. Five major transformational roles can be identified, although these may not be exclusive.Policy implementersPrimary care workforce reforms in Denmark and Finland illustrate that health workers’ perceptions matter for implementation. Health policy must create governance architectures that are capable of stimulating and supporting workforce-driven actions and integrating transformational capacities strategically into health policy agendas to achieve the desired outcomes. Governance research and theories [13] offer a broader framework for assessing the connections between bottom-up and top-down capacities and their effects, while meso-level approaches specify transformations in health system contexts.Research into professions, for instance, shows that governments in the past have used and nurtured the capacities of high-level professions strategically, mostly medicine, but hampered others [14]. Medical professions are integrated in European health systems, serving as mediators between the state and the citizens, policy implementors and service organizers. These capacities are strongest in social health insurance systems that assigned statutory rights to medical professions, but also matter in national health services and mixed systems. It places the linkage of upward (bureaucracy) and downward (street level) dynamics in a wider governance architecture and draws on available practical solutions that support realist and actionable policies, including sensitivity for political instability and vulnerabilities [12, 15]. Yet, it also highlights lessons to be learned for improving preparedness and protection of the workforce, and strengthening public health [16, 17] and health security [18]. Governments in Europe and beyond should urgently learn these lessons.

papers.title_original: Health and care workforce-driven transformations can improve workforce stability and strengthen health system resilience

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the need for a resilient health and care workforce to meet changing population health demands and new security threats, highlighting the lack of a coherent workforce strategy in most European countries.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a Viewpoint analyzing policy and system-level transformations in health and care workforce strategies, focusing on European countries and their health systems.
analysis.methods: The methods involve examining policy shifts, workforce capacities, and strategic governance architectures through case studies and examples of community health workers, nurse-led care, and other frontline initiatives.
analysis.main_results: The study identifies five major transformational roles of the health and care workforce, including policy implementers, system transformers, workforce stabilizers, social inclusion facilitators, and workforce-driven innovators, with examples from Denmark, Finland, Germany, and Czechia.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that recognizing the health and care workforce as an active player and essential pillar of health systems can lead to new capacities for stability and resilience, offering a novel perspective on workforce policy.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that shifting workforce policy to focus on capacities and integration can improve health system resilience, support policy implementation, and enhance equity and inclusiveness in healthcare provision.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on a Viewpoint, which may lack empirical data, and the study does not provide quantitative results, limiting the strength of the conclusions to a moderate level.

analysis.summary_en: This Viewpoint argues that health and care workforce-driven transformations are essential for improving workforce stability and strengthening health system resilience. It highlights the need for a shift from viewing health workers as mere infrastructure to recognizing their active role in policy implementation and system innovation. The study identifies five transformational roles, including policy implementers, system transformers, and social inclusion facilitators, with examples from various European countries. It emphasizes the importance of integrating these capacities into health policy agendas to address the workforce crisis and enhance preparedness. However, the evidence is based on a policy analysis rather than empirical data, limiting the strength of the conclusions to a moderate level.

papers.abstract_zh: 结论与政策方向健康和护理工作队伍政策危机要求对健康政策和体系进行根本性转变,将讨论重点转向能力和以工作队伍为中心的创新。四个主要的战略政策转变对于充分增强和整合变革性工作队伍能力具有指示意义。建立一个多层级的参与式治理架构,将一线工作人员的自下而上的能力和自信心与自上而下的战略指导相连接,更加协调和有效地利用现有知识和可操作的政策解决方案。将卫生体系和护理组织转向以社区和初级卫生保健为中心的方法,这些方法能够更好地激发自下而上的创新,并将以工作队伍驱动的知识战略性地整合到更广泛的卫生政策中。将工作队伍政策从以人力资源作为基础设施的技术方法,转向将卫生和护理工作人员视为个体,以及将工作队伍视为卫生体系安全和韧性的关键支柱。通过改善关于以工作队伍驱动的创新的数据和研究,创建能够整合变革性能力的治理架构,同时确保对工作队伍稳定性和卫生体系韧性的监管和战略监督。引言变化的人口健康状况和新的安全威胁要求一个有韧性的卫生和护理工作队伍,然而卫生工作者正面临疲惫,劳动力市场能力正在下降,大多数欧洲国家仍缺乏连贯的工作队伍战略。在这种情况下,以工作队伍驱动的稳定性和韧性可能会自下而上产生。然而,这些能力尚未被卫生政策充分理解。相反,卫生和护理工作人员大多被视为关键基础设施的一部分,而未被充分认识到其作为个体和工作队伍在卫生体系中的核心作用。

analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是一个观点,分析卫生和护理劳动力战略的政策和系统层面的转变,重点关注欧洲国家及其卫生系统。
analysis_zh.methods: 这些方法包括通过案例研究和社区卫生工作者、护士主导的护理和其他一线举措的例子来检查政策转变、劳动力能力和战略治理架构。
analysis_zh.main_results: 该研究以丹麦、芬兰、德国和捷克为例,确定了卫生和护理劳动力的五个主要转型角色,包括政策实施者、系统变革者、劳动力稳定者、社会包容促进者和劳动力驱动的创新者。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,认识到卫生和护理劳动力是卫生系统的积极参与者和重要支柱,可以带来新的稳定性和复原力能力,为劳动力政策提供新的视角。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,将劳动力政策转向关注能力和一体化可以提高卫生系统的弹性,支持政策实施,并增强医疗保健提供的公平性和包容性。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据基于观点,可能缺乏经验数据,并且研究没有提供定量结果,将结论的强度限制在中等水平。

news.content_title: Rabies reports are rising in California. The reason why is a mystery
news.content: Rabies reports are up across the United States this year, including in one greater Bay Area county where human exposures to rabid animals have tripled, prompting a local advisory to stay away from sick or injured creatures. Scientists can't yet explain the uptick in rabies, which could be due to climate change, more awareness among the public or some unknown factor. Nationally, the number of rabies inquiries after a potential exposure is up 17% this year over last, and use of post-exposure prophylaxis also has increased, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In Santa Cruz County, authorities have identified nine rabid bats so far this year. Last year and the year before, they recorded three, and in 2023, just one. In each case, at least one individual was exposed to the bat and needed treatment. "I don't find this increase alarming, but I do want to make people aware," said Dr. Maris Brenn-White, veterinarian for the Santa Cruz County Animal Shelter. "I want them to know that rabies is scary and we think there's more of it, but just don't touch wildlife and vaccinate your pets, and you don't need to worry about it." Rabies is rare but almost always fatal once a person develops symptoms; fewer than 10 Americans die of it every year. When someone does survive, it makes headlines . The disease once was spread mostly through dogs, but domestic dogs are now required by law to be vaccinated almost everywhere in the U.S., so most human cases are from bat bites or scratches; among pets, cats are much more likely than dogs to be infected. Last year, California reported more than 300 rabid bats, plus 19 skunks and a few foxes and cats. Statewide, there were 342 reports of rabid animals last year, and 368 so far this year. In the Bay Area, there were 48 rabies exposures reported last year and 47 so far this year, almost all of them wild animals but at least one domestic cat in Alameda County . The illness is caused by a virus that spreads via saliva. The virus attacks the nervous system, eventually getting into the brain. It causes widespread damage, eventually disabling basic body functions like breathing and swallowing. The incubation period can be weeks, and early symptoms include fever, headache and fatigue; once a person feels ill, they almost certainly will die. Post-exposure prophylaxis, though, is incredibly effective, and almost everyone who is treated will avoid illness. Treatment includes the rabies vaccine, which takes a couple of weeks to kick in, so patients also are given rabies immunoglobulin, a fast-acting antibody that provides immediate protection. The shots can be painful when they're injected directly into a wound, but they're not as awful as they once were, infectious disease experts said. "Rabies is endemic to California and the United States, so it's something always in the background," said Dr. Matt Willis, former Marin County health officer who now writes a Substack on public health statewide called Your Local Epidemiologist . He said typically about 10% of bats tested in Marin County are positive for rabies year after year, "so we know that we have this perpetual reservoir of this lethal virus very close by." They noted that rabies is rare enough that the increases reported so far this year are small and may be a one-off event. Perhaps, they said, cases will go down again next year. But most likely, there is something happening that is increasing exposures, several infectious disease experts said. Climate change could be a factor: Warm weather is known to increase viral reproduction, for example, so maybe there's more rabies virus in circulation. Bats may also reproduce more during hotter weather, which could lead to more human interactions. "I'm not going to pretend to have an answer" to the role of climate change on rabies, Willis said. The COVID-19 pandemic made many people more sensitive to the role of pathogens in the community, she said. And then this year, several outbreaks of infectious diseases have made headlines: hantavirus , Ebola , cyclospora . "I definitely think there's a component of 'we're awash in infectious disease,'" Gandhi said. "It could be that people are just getting more worried. It's a very scary time for infectious disease." Rabies, too, has been in the news more this year with several reports of unusual encounters between rabid animals and humans. The animals were not found, so it's not known if they were rabid, but both individuals had to get rabies shots. Each of the incidents alone is not necessarily striking, but to have them all in one summer is curious, infectious disease experts said. Still, said Dr. Dean Winslow, a Stanford infectious disease expert, "I'd be more concerned if there was a dramatic increase in exposure from cats and dogs." One scenario is waking up with a bat in the bedroom - that is cause for concern, infectious disease experts said, and people should contact a doctor and animal control in that case. news.content: Australians told to stop touching bats amid growing concern about deadly rabies-like virus Australian authorities are warning the public against touching bats after a sharp rise in bites and scratches raise concern about exposure to a rare virus that's almost always fatal once symptoms develop. NSW Health said on Tuesday that 43 people had been bitten or scratched by bats in northern parts of the state between 28 September and 10 October, compared with 10 during the same period last year. The incidents were reported across the Hunter Region, the Mid North Coast, northern NSW, and the Central Coast. Australian bat lyssavirus, a virus related to rabies, can cause a fatal illness in humans. There is no effective treatment once symptoms begin, although vaccination after exposure can help prevent disease. "We want people to assume that any bat could carry Australian bat lyssavirus, which is a close relative to the rabies virus and very dangerous to humans," said Keira Glasgow, director of health protection at NSW Health. "It is incredibly rare for Australian bat lyssavirus to transmit to humans, but once symptoms start in people who are scratched or bitten by an infected bat, sadly there's no effective treatment," she said. "If you are bitten or scratched by a bat, urgent medical assessment is crucial." People who are bitten or scratched should immediately wash the wound with soap and water for 15 minutes, apply an antiseptic with antiviral action, and seek urgent medical attention. The warning comes as wildlife experts report rising bat activity linked to food shortages. "Consequently members of the community are seeing flying foxes remaining in their backyard trees during the day," Ingrid Emery, executive director of conservation programmes at the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water, said, according to Nine. "This food shortage event is occurring along the eastern coast from the Clarence Valley in the north to the South Coast." lyssavirus is found in bats, including flying foxes, and is distinct from rabies, which isn't found in the country. The infection can cause flu-like symptoms, including fever and headache, before progressing to paralysis, delirium and seizures. Death usually occurs within a week or two of symptoms developing. Symptoms typically begin about a week after exposure but can sometimes take years to appear. Authorities are urging the public not to handle injured or grounded bats and to contact trained wildlife rescuers instead

news.content_zh: 由于咬伤和抓伤事件急剧增加,澳大利亚当局向公众发出警告,不要触摸蝙蝠,引发人们对接触致命的澳大利亚蝙蝠狂犬病病毒的担忧。据新南威尔士州卫生局称,2026年9月28日至10月10日期间,该州北部地区有43人被蝙蝠咬伤或抓伤,而去年同期有10人。据报道,猎人地区、中北海岸、新南威尔士州北部和中央海岸均发生了此类事件。该病毒与 狂犬病 相关,可导致人类致命疾病,一旦出现症状,狂犬病 就没有有效的治疗方法。然而,接触后的 疫苗接种 可能有助于预防该疾病。这一警告发出之际,野生动物专家指出,蝙蝠活动的增加与食物短缺有关,蝙蝠白天都呆在后院的树上。当局建议人们避免处理受伤或搁浅的蝙蝠,而是联系训练有素的野生动物救援人员。他们还建议用肥皂和水清洗伤口 15 分钟,使用具有 抗病毒药物 作用的消毒剂,并寻求紧急医疗救助。

news.content_title: New AI system accelerates rabies virus detection in cell cultures
news.content: Rabies virus detection in cell cultures could soon become faster and more accessible, thanks to a world-first AI system developed by researchers at the University of Surrey's Institute for People-Centred AI (PAI) in collaboration with the Rabies and Viral Zoonoses team at the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA). The breakthrough is designed to help improve surveillance of one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases and deliver practical, laboratory-ready tools that can be adopted in endemic countries. Despite being almost entirely preventable through vaccination, rabies causes around 59,000 human deaths every year. Current practices for diagnosis and measuring protective antibodies through vaccination still rely on specialists manually examining thousands of microscope images - which can be slow, labour-intensive and open to differences in interpretation. In a DEFRA-funded study published in Nature Scientific Reports, the research team created the first AI-based workflow capable of identifying rabies virus infection in cell cultures and accurately measuring antibody concentration levels. Using more than 2,300 fluorescence images containing over 36,000 annotated image sections, the team trained several deep learning models to recognize rabies virus infection within cells. The best-performing model correctly classified 99.6 per cent of samples and almost perfectly distinguished infected from uninfected cells, avoiding false alarms. Joan Amaya-Cuesta, PhD researcher at the University of Surrey and Rabies and Viral Zoonoses Research Scientist at the APHA, said: Rabies is one of the world's oldest and deadliest infectious diseases, claiming tens of thousands of lives every year because timely diagnosis and surveillance remain challenging in many parts of the world. Once clinical signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so prevention and early diagnosis are essential. Our AI workflow provides laboratories with a faster and more consistent way to analyze samples while reducing the reliance on manual interpretation." Joan Amaya-Cuesta, PhD researcher, University of Surrey and Rabies and Viral Zoonoses Research Scientist at the APHA The technology could help laboratories analyze samples more quickly and consistently, particularly in countries where rabies remains endemic and specialist expertise is limited. It could also reliably measure antibody levels used to assess vaccine protection and support international pet travel requirements. Professor Miroslaw Bober, Professor of Video Processing and Machine Intelligence at the University of Surrey, said: We recommend - VIEW VIDEO: Dr. Kari Fisher discusses obesity in adult patients aged 65 years or older Sponsored by Lilly USA, LLC. - WATCH NOW: Kari Fisher, DNP, reviews information on the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program Sponsored by Lilly USA, LLC. - VIEW VIDEO: Doctor discusses obesity in adult patients aged 65 years or older Sponsored by Lilly USA, LLC. - VIEW VIDEO: Kari Fisher, DNP, reviews obesity in adult patients aged 65 years or older Sponsored by Lilly USA, LLC. "This research shows how AI can support scientists by carrying out complex image analysis quickly, consistently and at scale. While we've demonstrated this approach for rabies, the same framework could be applied to other infectious diseases that rely on similar laboratory tests, helping researchers and diagnostic laboratories make better use of AI in the future." The results establish a framework that can be adapted for the detection, analysis, and surveillance of other pathogens, supporting broader applications of AI across infectious disease research and diagnostics. We hope this innovation will help strengthen rabies surveillance and, ultimately, support global efforts to eliminate human deaths from this disease. This technology is now being further developed for use to detect the virus in infected brain tissue which we hope will transform international rabies diagnostic laboratories." Dr. Lorraine M. McElhinney, Head of the National Reference Laboratory for Human and Animal Rabies at the APHA Amaya-Cuesta, J., et al. (2026) Deep learning enables rabies virus detection and antibody quantification in cell culture. Scientific Reports. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, October 14, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Rabies Vaccine Delays Endanger Bite Victims in Rural Ethiopia by October 14, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Rabies Vaccine Delays Endanger Bite Victims in Rural Ethiopia Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In the Gondar zones of northwestern Ethiopia, a new study has revealed a troubling paradox at the heart of rabies prevention: although nearly all dog bite victims surveyed knew that rabies is a fatal disease and that vaccination after exposure can save their lives, the overwhelming majority still waited far too long before receiving their first dose. The research, published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases, found that 86.1 percent of bite victims delayed initiating post-exposure vaccination beyond the critical 48-hour window, a figure that public health experts describe as alarmingly high even by the standards of rabies-endemic regions. The study, led by Bezawit Kassaw Hailu and colleagues, set out to quantify how long victims of dog bites wait before beginning post-exposure vaccination, known clinically as PEV, and to identify the factors that influence that timing. Between January and June 2025, the researchers conducted face-to-face interviews with 260 dog bite victims or their guardians across the Gondar zones. The team defined delayed initiation as beginning vaccination more than 48 hours after the exposure incident, a threshold grounded in the biology of the rabies virus, which travels along peripheral nerves toward the central nervous system and can reach the brain before protective immunity develops if prophylaxis is postponed. Discover more Shop African Art Get Tested Read Med Journals The numbers were stark. Of the 260 participants, only 36, or 13.9 percent, commenced vaccination within 48 hours of being bitten. The remaining 224 individuals, representing 86.1 percent of the cohort, crossed the two-day threshold before receiving their first injection. Because rabies is virtually 100 percent fatal once clinical symptoms appear, and because post-exposure prophylaxis is among the most effective interventions in all of medicine when administered promptly, every hour of delay narrows the window in which the vaccine can reliably intercept the virus on its journey to the nervous system. Discover more Find Pet Care Vaccine vaccines vaccine What makes the finding especially striking is the knowledge landscape the researchers documented. A majority of respondents, 88.5 percent, were aware that rabies exists in their area. Some 71.5 percent could identify the signs of the disease, 75.4 percent knew how it is transmitted, and an overwhelming 96.5 percent understood its fatal nature. Even more encouraging, 95.4 percent recognized the need for post-exposure vaccination after a bite. Knowledge of the disease itself, in other words, was widespread and remarkably detailed for a rural setting where health literacy resources are often scarce. Attitudes toward the vaccine were similarly favorable. A majority of respondents believed the cost of the vaccine was fair, and 95 percent considered post-exposure prophylaxis effective. When the researchers probed the reasons for delay, cost of vaccination emerged as a barrier for only a minority of participants; 76.2 percent said the expense was not a reason they postponed treatment. This combination of high awareness, positive attitudes toward vaccination, and minimal financial barriers presents a genuine scientific puzzle: if victims know the disease is deadly, know the vaccine works, and do not cite cost as an obstacle, why do so few seek timely care? The authors’ conclusion points toward a critical gap in understanding. Respondents, they suggest, may simply not be aware of the risk posed by delay itself. Knowing that rabies kills and knowing that a vaccine exists are not the same as knowing that the effectiveness of that vaccine is time-sensitive, and that the difference between seeking care on the day of the bite and two days later can be the difference between survival and death. Health messaging in endemic regions has traditionally emphasized the lethality of rabies and the availability of treatment, but this study indicates that the urgency of timing has not been communicated with comparable force. Using logistic regression models, the researchers identified two factors significantly associated with the timing of vaccination initiation. The first was the severity of the bite. Victims who suffered deep bites were substantially less likely to delay, with an odds ratio of 0.22 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.07 to 0.66, and a P value of 0.008. In practical terms, a deep bite more than halved the odds of postponement compared with superficial wounds. This pattern is consistent with the intuitive logic of threat perception: the more dramatic and painful the injury, the more urgently the victim recognizes the danger and seeks medical attention. Discover more Check Symptoms Find Vaccines Book Vet Visits Buy Maps Explore History The second significant factor was the ownership of the biting animal. People bitten by stray dogs were also less likely to delay initiation of vaccination, with an odds ratio of 0.51, a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.27 to 0.95, and a P value of 0.033. This finding may seem counterintuitive at first glance, since stray dogs cannot be observed for signs of illness the way a neighbor’s vaccinated pet can. But it makes sense in the context of risk assessment: a bite from an unknown, unowned animal carries unmistakable uncertainty about the animal’s rabies status, prompting swifter action, whereas a bite from a familiar dog may lull victims into a false sense of security, encouraging them to wait and watch the animal for symptoms that may never become obvious before the virus has already taken hold. The implications of these findings extend well beyond the Gondar zones. Rabies remains one of the most lethal zoonotic diseases worldwide, claiming an estimated tens of thousands of lives annually, with the vast majority of deaths occurring in Asia and Africa and with children in rural communities bearing a disproportionate burden. The virus is a lyssavirus transmitted through the saliva of infected mammals, most commonly dogs, and it hijacks peripheral nerve fibers to reach the central nervous system. Once neurological symptoms such as hydrophobia, agitation, and paralysis begin, no treatment has ever been shown to halt the disease. Post-exposure prophylaxis, which combines wound washing, rabies vaccine doses, and in severe cases rabies immunoglobulin, works because it stimulates immunity during the days or weeks the virus spends traveling from the wound site to the brain. That window, however, is finite, and every study that documents delay in initiation helps explain why deaths persist in regions where vaccines are nominally available. The Ethiopian study’s authors conclude that the high rate of delay, despite widespread knowledge and few reported barriers, underscores the need for interventions focused specifically on the risk of delayed PEV initiation. Such interventions might include community education campaigns that emphasize the 48-hour benchmark as explicitly as they emphasize the disease’s fatality, integration of bite management guidance into school and community health programs, and strengthening of access points so that victims can reach vaccination services quickly when the urgency is understood. The research also highlights the value of targeting messaging toward owners of domestic dogs, who may underestimate risk when the biting animal is familiar. As the authors note, respondents in their study knew many aspects of rabies control and faced fewer barriers to uptake than might have been expected, yet delay remained the norm rather than the exception. Closing that gap between knowledge and timely action may prove to be one of the most important steps toward reducing rabies deaths in Ethiopia and across the endemic world. The research, published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases, found that 86.1 percent of bite victims delayed initiating post-exposure vaccination beyond the critical 48-hour window, a figure that public health experts describe as alarmingly high even by the standards of rabies-endemic regions. The study, led by Bezawit Kassaw Hailu and colleagues, set out to quantify how long victims of dog bites wait before beginning post-exposure vaccination, known clinically as PEV, and to identify the factors that influence that timing. Between January and June 2025, the researchers conducted face-to-face interviews with 260 dog bite victims or their guardians across the Gondar zones. The team defined delayed initiation as beginning vaccination more than 48 hours after the exposure incident, a threshold grounded in the biology of the rabies virus, which travels along peripheral nerves toward the central nervous system and can reach the brain before protective immunity develops if prophylaxis is postponed. Discover more Shop African Art Get Tested Read Med Journals The numbers were stark. Of the 260 participants, only 36, or 13.9 percent, commenced vaccination within 48 hours of being bitten. The remaining 224 individuals, representing 86.1 percent of the cohort, crossed the two-day threshold before receiving their first injection. Because rabies is virtually 100 percent fatal once clinical symptoms appear, and because post-exposure prophylaxis is among the most effective interventions in all of medicine when administered promptly, every hour of delay narrows the window in which the vaccine can reliably intercept the virus on its journey to the nervous system. Discover more Find Pet Care Vaccine vaccines vaccine What makes the finding especially striking is the knowledge landscape the researchers documented. A majority of respondents, 88.5 percent, were aware that rabies exists in their area. Some 71.5 percent could identify the signs of the disease, 75.4 percent knew how it is transmitted, and an overwhelming 96.5 percent understood its fatal nature. Even more encouraging, 95.4 percent recognized the need for post-exposure vaccination after a bite. Knowledge of the disease itself, in other words, was widespread and remarkably detailed for a rural setting where health literacy resources are often scarce. Attitudes toward the vaccine were similarly favorable. A majority of respondents believed the cost of the vaccine was fair, and 95 percent considered post-exposure prophylaxis effective. When the researchers probed the reasons for delay, cost of vaccination emerged as a barrier for only a minority of participants; 76.2 percent said the expense was not a reason they postponed treatment. This combination of high awareness, positive attitudes toward vaccination, and minimal financial barriers presents a genuine scientific puzzle: if victims know the disease is deadly, know the vaccine works, and do not cite cost as an obstacle, why do so few seek timely care? The authors’ conclusion points toward a critical gap in understanding. Respondents, they suggest, may simply not be aware of the risk posed by delay itself. Knowing that rabies kills and knowing that a vaccine exists are not the same as knowing that the effectiveness of that vaccine is time-sensitive, and that the difference between seeking care on the day of the bite and two days later can be the difference between survival and death. Health messaging in endemic regions has traditionally emphasized the lethality of rabies and the availability of treatment, but this study indicates that the urgency of timing has not been communicated with comparable force. Using logistic regression models, the researchers identified two factors significantly associated with the timing of vaccination initiation. The first was the severity of the bite. Victims who suffered deep bites were substantially less likely to delay, with an odds ratio of 0.22 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.07 to 0.66, and a P value of 0.008. In practical terms, a deep bite more than halved the odds of postponement compared with superficial wounds. This pattern is consistent with the intuitive logic of threat perception: the more dramatic and painful the injury, the more urgently the victim recognizes the danger and seeks medical attention. Discover more Check Symptoms Find Vaccines Book Vet Visits Buy Maps Explore History The second significant factor was the ownership of the biting animal. People bitten by stray dogs were also less likely to delay initiation of vaccination, with an odds ratio of 0.51, a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.27 to 0.95, and a P value of 0.033. This finding may seem counterintuitive at first glance, since stray dogs cannot be observed for signs of illness the way a neighbor’s vaccinated pet can. But it makes sense in the context of risk assessment: a bite from an unknown, unowned animal carries unmistakable uncertainty about the animal’s rabies status, prompting swifter action, whereas a bite from a familiar dog may lull victims into a false sense of security, encouraging them to wait and watch the animal for symptoms that may never become obvious before the virus has already taken hold. The implications of these findings extend well beyond the Gondar zones. Rabies remains one of the most lethal zoonotic diseases worldwide, claiming an estimated tens of thousands of lives annually, with the vast majority of deaths occurring in Asia and Africa and with children in rural communities bearing a disproportionate burden. The virus is a lyssavirus transmitted through the saliva of infected mammals, most commonly dogs, and it hijacks peripheral nerve fibers to reach the central nervous system. Once neurological symptoms such as hydrophobia, agitation, and paralysis begin, no treatment has ever been shown to halt the disease. Post-exposure prophylaxis, which combines wound washing, rabies vaccine doses, and in severe cases rabies immunoglobulin, works because it stimulates immunity during the days or weeks the virus spends traveling from the wound site to the brain. That window, however, is finite, and every study that documents delay in initiation helps explain why deaths persist in regions where vaccines are nominally available. The Ethiopian study’s authors conclude that the high rate of delay, despite widespread knowledge and few reported barriers, underscores the need for interventions focused specifically on the risk of delayed PEV initiation. Such interventions might include community education campaigns that emphasize the 48-hour benchmark as explicitly as they emphasize the disease’s fatality, integration of bite management guidance into school and community health programs, and strengthening of access points so that victims can reach vaccination services quickly when the urgency is understood. The research also highlights the value of targeting messaging toward owners of domestic dogs, who may underestimate risk when the biting animal is familiar. As the authors note, respondents in their study knew many aspects of rabies control and faced fewer barriers to uptake than might have been expected, yet delay remained the norm rather than the exception. Closing that gap between knowledge and timely action may prove to be one of the most important steps toward reducing rabies deaths in Ethiopia and across the endemic world. Take steps now to protect tender plants from the cold. && Close Featured Heat, rain likely fueled Clark County's first West Nile case, bat rabies since 2021 Jessica Orozco - Staff Writer Jessica Orozco Staff Writer Author email Oct 14, 2026 Oct 14, 2026 Updated Oct 14, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Print Copy article link Save A man walks out of the Clark County Health Department on Home Road in Springfield on Aug. 14, 2026. Hotter temperatures and wetter weather could be contributing factors to the first human case of West Nile Virus and positive bat rabies test in Clark County since 2021, according to the health department. JESSICA OROZCO / STAFF According to the health department, unseasonably hot and wet weather may have fueled Clark County’s first human case of West Nile virus and positive bat rabies test since 2021. The Clark County Health Department announced Sept. 30 that a bat in Medway tested positive for rabies and one person on the southern side of the Elmwood Place neighborhood in Springfield tested positive for West Nile virus. Health Commissioner Chris Cook noted that the occurrence does not appear to be part of a broader trend, potentially mirroring 2021, when both diseases surfaced coincidentally at the same time. However, prolonged high temperatures and increased rainfall could boost mosquito populations, the primary carriers of West Nile virus. A Frisbee full of water can be a breeding ground for thousands of mosquito eggs, Cook said. Any standing water should be emptied or treated to avoid mosquito propagation. More artificial light at night is attractive to a particular breed of mosquitoes, as are “urban heat islands,” which are urban areas with more pavement and manufacturing that produce heat, Cook said. This extends the biting season. “They raise the temperature in this dome area anywhere between 1 and 7 degrees, and when you have warmer temperatures, viruses like West Nile virus actually do propagate better,” Cook said. “And you’ve got a lengthened warm season.” There has been one reported human case of West Nile virus in Montgomery County in 2026, and in 2025, there were four human cases reported, according to Public Health-Dayton & Montgomery County. Greene and Miami counties have also each had one human case of West Nile virus this year, according to the Ohio Department of Health’s infectious diseases dashboard. About 80% of people with West Nile virus are asymptomatic, and there is no way to know before contracting the virus if a person will become severely ill. People who are symptomatic will begin feeling sick from three to 14 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito, according to the health department. Most symptomatic people have mild symptoms like fever, headache, body aches, vomiting, diarrhea, rash and swollen glands. These usually last anywhere from a few days to a week. About 1 in 150 people will develop severe illness, which can include symptoms like high fever, headache, neck stiffness, muscle weakness, tremors, seizures, disorientation, paralysis and coma. These can last several weeks with the possibility for lasting neurological effects. There is no specific treatment for the virus and no vaccine. Preventing mosquito bites is the best way to avoid West Nile virus. This means using an EPA-registered insect repellent that contains DEET or Picaridin even if outdoors exposure is limited, Cook said. Mosquitoes can carry other diseases, too, so preventing bites is crucial. “Mosquitoes are a really good vector for a lot of different things,” Deputy Health Commissioner Gracie Hemphill said. “Nothing is popping up right now trends(-wise) but mosquitoes can be nasty little bugs.” No human rabies cases have been reported in Ohio since 1970, noted Megan Davis, director of environmental health. She added that the health department has recently submitted an increased number of bats to the Ohio Department of Health for testing. Ohio typically records about 30 positive rabies cases in mammals each year, but that number has risen to 56, all of them bats, Cook said. Increased media coverage of rabies likely encourages people to report encounters with bats and have them tested rather than discarding them, Cook said. Rabies is almost 100% preventable if treated immediately. But it is almost 100% fatal after symptoms start, Hemphill said. The health department can capture a bat and send it off for testing, Davis said. She warned people against touching a bat without bite-resistant gloves. If a person is bit by a bat or was in an enclosed area with one and does not know for certain whether they were bitten, they should wash the area for 15 minutes and then seek medical care, Cook said. That care starts with an injection of human rabies immune cobalamin directly into a wound or where a person handled the bat. That is followed by a series of four immunizations over a two-week period. Megan Davis, director of environmental health at the Clark County Health Department, holds an insulated cooler that is used to pack and ship rabies specimens to the Ohio Department of Health’s laboratory. JOSEPH COOKE / STAFF JOSEPH COOKE / STAFF Davis said all openings in the home like chimneys, attics and window screens should be properly sealed, and pets like dogs, cats and ferrets should be up to date on their rabies vaccinations. Prevention is key for both West Nile virus and rabies, Cook said. “While we’ve got a couple of those blips on the radar here, with West Nile virus and rabies, we’ve lived with them for years,” Cook said. “It’s just about respecting the risks that Mother Nature presents to us and making sure that we engage with prevention activities.” Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Jessica Orozco Staff Writer Author email Latest News Local Vice provost to be University of Dayton’s interim provost in presidential transition Local Dayton Dragons to host Banana Ball game during 2027 season Local Calendar: Things to do in Springfield and surrounding areas, Oct. 15-21 Local Clark County Common Pleas Court cases Local Clark County Municipal Court cases Most Read Lifestyles Best of Springfield 2026: See the list of winners Local These 15 people were indicted in Clark County Local 2 injured in Springfield shooting Local New Enon administrator is a retired Springfield fire chief Local Northwestern investigating reports students told to lift shirts to check for cell phones

supplementary_news.content_title: New AI system accelerates rabies virus detection in cell cultures
supplementary_news.content: Rabies virus detection in cell cultures could soon become faster and more accessible, thanks to a world-first AI system developed by researchers at the University of Surrey's Institute for People-Centred AI (PAI) in collaboration with the Rabies and Viral Zoonoses team at the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA). The breakthrough is designed to help improve surveillance of one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases and deliver practical, laboratory-ready tools that can be adopted in endemic countries. Despite being almost entirely preventable through vaccination, rabies causes around 59,000 human deaths every year. Current practices for diagnosis and measuring protective antibodies through vaccination still rely on specialists manually examining thousands of microscope images - which can be slow, labour-intensive and open to differences in interpretation. In a DEFRA-funded study published in Nature Scientific Reports, the research team created the first AI-based workflow capable of identifying rabies virus infection in cell cultures and accurately measuring antibody concentration levels. Using more than 2,300 fluorescence images containing over 36,000 annotated image sections, the team trained several deep learning models to recognize rabies virus infection within cells. The best-performing model correctly classified 99.6 per cent of samples and almost perfectly distinguished infected from uninfected cells, avoiding false alarms. Joan Amaya-Cuesta, PhD researcher at the University of Surrey and Rabies and Viral Zoonoses Research Scientist at the APHA, said: Rabies is one of the world's oldest and deadliest infectious diseases, claiming tens of thousands of lives every year because timely diagnosis and surveillance remain challenging in many parts of the world. Once clinical signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so prevention and early diagnosis are essential. Our AI workflow provides laboratories with a faster and more consistent way to analyze samples while reducing the reliance on manual interpretation." Joan Amaya-Cuesta, PhD researcher, University of Surrey and Rabies and Viral Zoonoses Research Scientist at the APHA The technology could help laboratories analyze samples more quickly and consistently, particularly in countries where rabies remains endemic and specialist expertise is limited. It could also reliably measure antibody levels used to assess vaccine protection and support international pet travel requirements. Professor Miroslaw Bober, Professor of Video Processing and Machine Intelligence at the University of Surrey, said: "This research shows how AI can support scientists by carrying out complex image analysis quickly, consistently and at scale. While we've demonstrated this approach for rabies, the same framework could be applied to other infectious diseases that rely on similar laboratory tests, helping researchers and diagnostic laboratories make better use of AI in the future." The results establish a framework that can be adapted for the detection, analysis, and surveillance of other pathogens, supporting broader applications of AI across infectious disease research and diagnostics. We hope this innovation will help strengthen rabies surveillance and, ultimately, support global efforts to eliminate human deaths from this disease. This technology is now being further developed for use to detect the virus in infected brain tissue which we hope will transform international rabies diagnostic laboratories." Dr. Lorraine M. McElhinney, Head of the National Reference Laboratory for Human and Animal Rabies at the APHA Source: Journal reference: Amaya-Cuesta, J., et al. (2026) Deep learning enables rabies virus detection and antibody quantification in cell culture. Scientific Reports . DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-57955-8. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-57955-8
